newsitem.title: USA: Scientists count minutes to historic Mars landing.
newsitem.headline: Scientists count minutes to historic Mars landing.

text.p: Scientists waited anxiously on Friday as the Pathfinder space probe neared a landing on Mars, the first time an American craft has reached the Red Planet in 21 years.

The Jet Propulsion Laboratory where the flight was controlled and monitored was a hive of activity as the countdown to the landing progressed. The craft was scheduled to land on Mars at 1:07 p.m. EDT (1507 GMT).

Mission Manager Richard Cook described the mood among the 200 specialists at the lab, who have guided Pathfinder and its valuable "Mars Buggy" cargo on its 309-million-mile (497 million km) journey to Mars, as "happy, anxious and nervous."

"Things are going amazingly smoothly. It's been an easy cruise (to Mars) and the spacecraft is performing extremely well. We are confident that the actual landing process will go well," Cook said. "The team is chomping at the bit and anxious to get on with it. We're all a little bit nervous but when we get into it that will disappear," he added.

The spacecraft was to become the first ever to pierce the atmosphere of another planet without initially orbiting it. Another space first involved the parachute set to deploy while Pathfinder was still travelling at a supersonic speed of 1,000 mph (1,600 kph), a manoeuvre never performed in space.

Another piece of equipment never before tested in space were the crucial airbags surrounding the Mars lander portion of the craft, which were to be inflated just eight seconds before landing to cushion the craft as hit hit the Martian surface at about 45 to 55 mph (72 to 88 kph).

The lander itself is also unique. The bags will cause it to bounce several times in the thin Martian atmosphere, at first as high as a four-story building and as far as 100 yards (metres) with each bounce before it finally comes to a rest.

The airbags must then be deflated and the craft's three "petals" or pads must open up to allow the Mars Rover to roll out on to the Martian surface, the first time a remote controlled buggy has roamed the surface of another planet.

The landing module was to hit Martian soil just four minutes after slamming into the Red Planet's atmosphere at 16,000 mph (25,740 kph) but scientists will not know if the landing has been successful for four more hours. Scientists said Earth will be on the Martian horizon during the landing and no communication with the spacecraft will be possible.

Scientists also readily admit that America's latest venture to Mars -- the first since a Viking mission landed there in 1976 and took blurry black-and-white pictures -- is as full of hazards as Mars' crater-pockmarked surface.

"We don't really know where we are landing, we don't know what sort of terrain we are landing in, and we don't know what the atmosphere will be," explained Brian Muirhead, deputy project manager for the mission who is also in charge of managing how the flight goes, right down to the landing.
In fact, Pathfinder will not be landing where scientists first thought it would.

Mission manager Cook, looking weary after a full night of plotting the spacecraft's course, told reporters a trajectory correction manoeuvre performed several days ago had given it a shallower entry mode into the Martian atmosphere, meaning it would travel further and land 28 miles (45 km) from the original landing site.
Cook stressed that the new landing site was as safe as the original and posed no problems for the success of the mission, which is to analyse rocks and soil and record weather conditions.
